Project journal · 29 October — 5 November 2026

CalibratedFrom a scanned hallway to a changing reality.

A physically walked VR installation built around a simple starting condition: the visible hallway should coincide with the real one. The development process then asks how that familiar space can turn, open and disappear around the participant.

A concise account of the key choices, illustrated with nine original pictures supplied during agent conversations. All dates and times use Zurich time (CET, UTC+1). Historical cutoff: 05 Nov 2026 12:08 CET.

The decisions that shaped the project

Render on the PC; use Steam Link.Chrome + SteamVR/OpenXR → Steam Link → Quest 3 became the only active route after presentation failures with Meta Link.

Move the scan, preserve physical tracking.Calibration transforms the environment; the tracked camera and controllers retain their real poses. Metric scale and independent alignment still require physical checks.

Protect manually adjusted placement.Keep scan placement in scanAsset.ts unchanged without permission. Configure scan landmark correspondences separately in landmarks.ts.

One behavior for buttons, preview and VR.Prototype through desktop controls, then automate those same actions with headset triggers. Freeze fitted geometry before movement.

Make pacing repeatable and audio continuous.Restart the sequence on recalibration. Use supplied recordings, queue speech, and keep ambience or transition music playing under effects.

Use screenshot feedback to refine the illusion.Exact centring, wall alignment, connected openings and irregular disintegration emerged through annotated views and repeated corrections.

The development process

0129 October

First, make the scan visible.

The work starts as a Gaussian-splat viewer built with agents in VS Code. An early three-copy PLY test establishes rendering; the project is consolidated into one repository. Black screens, immersive-session startup, scan orientation and the starting point become the first practical problems to solve.

022–3 November

Find a working PC-to-headset route.

A session can appear to start while the headset shows only a spinner. The recorded diagnosis identifies the projection-layer path as the problem on this setup; the classic XRWebGLLayer path enables the SteamVR/Steam Link route.

02 Nov 2026 14:15 CET · Classic-layer fix specified
03 Nov 2026 10:02 CET · SteamVR/Steam Link chosen as the sole active route

The user confirms that an iteration works on hardware. That establishes a working route, while measured calibration accuracy and later integrated behavior remain separate questions.

Source messages & timestamps
02 Nov 2026 14:15 CET
Goal: Make WebXR VR work in a three.js + Spark (sparkjs, Gaussian splats) app on desktop Chrome/Edge in PCVR (Quest 3 via SteamVR / Steam Link, OpenXR), without breaking the standalone Quest browser. Background (verified by testing on the target machine): - With three.js's standard VRButton, the XR session starts but the runtime never delivers a single XR frame -> headset shows a spinner, then "page not responding". - Cause: three.js WebXRManager uses the WebXR Layers path (XRWebGLBinding. createProjectionLayer) whenever `session.renderState.layers !== undefined`, and VRButton always adds 'layers' to optionalFeatures. Desktop Chrome exposes renderState.layers even when 'layers' was NOT requested. On this PCVR setup the projection-layer path delivers no frames. - The classic XRWebGLLayer path works (confirmed with three.js and raw WebGL). - Working fix used in the test page: create the session WITHOUT 'layers' and hide renderState.layers on that session instance, so three.js falls back to XRWebGLLayer: const session = await navigator.xr.requestSession('immersive-vr', { optionalFeatures: ['local-floor'] }); const getRS = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(XRSession.prototype, 'renderState').get; Object.defineProperty(session, 'renderState', { configurable: true, get() { const rs = getRS.call(this); return new Proxy(rs, { get(t, k) { if (k === 'layers') return undefined; const v = t[k]; return typeof v === 'function' ? v.bind(t) : v; }}); } }); await renderer.xr.setSession(session); Tasks: 1. Check the three.js version in the project. If that version offers an official way to disable the layers/projection-layer path, use it instead of the Proxy hack. Otherwise implement the hack above, scoped to the single session instance (never patch XRSession.prototype globally). 2. Replace three.js's VRButton with our own small "Enter VR / Exit VR" button module (e.g. src/xr/enterVR.js) that: - requests 'immersive-vr' with optionalFeatures ['local-floor', 'bounded-floor'] and NOT 'layers' when the classic path is chosen, - applies the renderState.layers hiding only in that case, - handles session end, button state, and "WebXR not available". 3. Make the layer path selectable: - Default: classic XRWebGLLayer on desktop (PCVR). - Keep the projection-layer path (standard behaviour incl. 'layers') on the standalone Quest browser (detect via user agent "OculusBrowser"), where it works and is faster. - URL override for testing: ?xrLayers=1 forces layers, ?xrLayers=0 forces classic. 4. Create the WebGL2 context ourselves, XR-compatible on the discrete GPU, and pass it to the renderer: const ctx = canvas.getContext('webgl2', { xrCompatible: true, antialias: false, powerPreference: 'high-performance' }); new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas, context: ctx }); (antialias off is usually right for splats; keep it configurable.) 5. Spark integration: - Check whether Spark ships its own XR / VR button or XR helper. If it does, make sure it goes through our enterVR() (or apply the same no-layers logic), so it doesn't silently request 'layers'. - Verify the SparkRenderer / splat sorting runs correctly during XR (stereo cameras, per-eye rendering, animation loop via renderer.setAnimationLoop). - Set renderer.xr.setFramebufferScaleFactor() BEFORE entering VR; expose it as a setting, since splat rendering is fill-rate heavy. 6. Add lightweight diagnostics (console + optional on-screen overlay behind ?xrDebug=1): GPU renderer string, which layer path was used, "first XR frame rendered", and a 5-second watchdog warning "no XR frames delivered". 7. Do not resize the renderer while renderer.xr.isPresenting. Acceptance criteria: - Desktop Chrome + SteamVR (Steam Link) on the PCVR machine: Enter VR shows the splat scene in the headset; the debug overlay shows the XRWebGLLayer path and frames counting. - Quest browser: still enters VR (projection layer path). - No global prototype patching; the workaround is isolated in one module with a comment explaining why it exists.

043–4 November

Turn the calibrated space into an installation.

The initial narrative asks the participant to find purpose and claim an education: whispered voices, a box and a ceiling badge lead into a 180-degree hallway reversal. The next prototype simplifies the trigger to a centred box with a fixed rotation pivot and manual desktop buttons. Physical box dimensions are set to 36 × 36 × 43 cm.

064–5 November

Make the sequence coherent and repeatable.

The user replaces generated ElevenLabs voices with supplied local music, speech and sound effects. Four ambience stages are joined by three transitions that anticipate the major changes. Speech stays intelligible over the bed; music should continue through wall movement and visual hitches.

05 Nov 2026 09:42 CET · Make passage through the rotated hallway reversible
05 Nov 2026 11:22 CET · Prepare the concealed hole before player passage

Recalibration restarts the game from zero. The second box arms an unseen wall reveal; gaze and physical passage control its movement and disappearance. The hole keeps its planned wall-relative position even if the participant crosses early. Return passage reverses the quarter-turn without restarting the story.

Replace clean effects with a convincing breakdown.

05 Nov 2026 11:50 CET · Reject a perfectly cut void

The latest visual correction asks for roughly five blast sites on each wall, progressing from far away toward the participant. Each blast should begin an uneven, local loss of Gaussians with rumbling, leaving organic patches instead of a uniform cut. This is a requested revision at the recorded cutoff.

What this record establishes

The overall process is iterative: establish rendering and hardware access, stabilise registration, prototype manually, connect the same actions into a repeatable sequence, then refine the illusion with screenshot feedback.

This document summarises the archived conversations through 05 Nov 2026 12:08 CET. Later changes are outside this historical snapshot. User-reported headset observations, automated software checks and measured physical alignment are distinct; the archive does not establish final registration accuracy, audio routing, stereo comfort or completion of every recent request.

The source collection contains 62 local Codex/OpenCode threads and 24 unique supplied pictures. Nine selected pictures, their accompanying messages and the source excerpts above are embedded here. Expand a source note to read the original wording; select a picture to enlarge it. This file needs no internet connection or companion folder.
